title: TB8-06369
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness (the Minister) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated February 1, 2018, that determined that the XXXX XXXX, citizen of Georgia, is a Convention refugee.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness (the Minister) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated February 1, 2018, that determined that the XXXX XXXX, citizen of Georgia, is a Convention refugee.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is a Convention refugee, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The Respondent is a fifty-one year old women from Georgia who was granted refugee protection as a victim of domestic violence. She first tried to travel to Canada in XXXX 2016 with a fraudulent Canadian passport, but was turned back in Cuba before the document was seized in Germany. She tried again to come to Canada with a false passport the following month. This time she was successful and was able to claim asylum at the airport upon her arrival. The RPD concluded that her testimony and documentary evidence was internally consistent. No adverse credibility findings were made and the RPD concluded that her narrative is likely true.

The Respondent did not disclose her previous failed attempt to come to Canada with a false passport under a different identity. This fact only came to light as the result of a database check conducted by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA). As a result of this discovery, the Minister intervened in writing on the basis the Respondent ought to be excluded from refugee protection by application of article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention as incorporated into the IRPA by section 98. The Minister argued that the Respondent's use of a fraudulent Canadian passport is a non-political crime committed before arrival in Canada that is sufficiently serious to warrant exclusion. The Respondent admitted that the allegation is true, but explained that she did not disclose this information because she was nervous and afraid. The RPD allowed her claim for protection on the basis of credibility and a finding that a crime was not committed.

The Minister objects to the RPD's positive determination on two grounds. First, the RPD erred in its interpretation and application of the law pertaining to article 1F(b) exclusion. Second, the RPD failed to take the Respondent's lack of truthfulness into account in finding that she is credible.

The standard of review for appeals to the RAD is that of correctness, unless deference should be shown to the RPD because it enjoyed a meaningful advantage over the RAD. No issue was identified to which deference should be shown on this basis.1
No new evidence was filed and no request was made for an oral hearing. ANALYSIS The RPD did not err in determining that the Respondent is credible

The RPD applied Chairperson's Guideline 4, Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-related Persecution and took note of the psychiatric report. After reviewing the supporting documentation and oral testimony, the Respondent was found to be credible.

Because this claim involves allegations of domestic violence, the RPD considered Chairperson's Guideline 4, Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-related Persecution. The psychiatric report was also considered. The panel noted the Minister's submission that the Respondent engaged in a deliberate attempt to mislead the RPD and that this should be taken into account in assessing credibility. The panel proceeded to conclude that the Respondent is not described in article 1F(b) of the Convention, but failed to account for this in the credibility assessment. The RPD went on to say that it had no major or identifiable concerns with the evidence submitted, but failed to account for the documents pertaining to the false passport in its reasons.

The RPD made two findings with respect to the use of a forged passport. First, the panel accepted the Respondent's testimony that she used it for the purpose of claiming asylum in Canada. Because she was proceeding to Canada through transit countries, the panel concluded that her conduct is not demonstrative of a lack of subjective fear. The RPD found her to be credible with respect to her subjective fear. The RPD then went on to conclude that her use of the false passport is not an offence by virtue of section 133 of the IRPA.

There is a difference between findings of fact made on a balance of probabilities standard and an assessment of whether the facts, as determined, establish a lack of subjective fear. The RPD confused the two steps by assessing the credibility of a subjective fear. What the RPD appears to have meant was that the Respondent's testimony was accepted as being true, and that the evidence, as established, demonstrates a subjective fear of persecution. As a result of this methodological error, the Minister is correct in submitting that the RPD failed to account for the use of the false passport in its credibility assessment, given that this only figures in its subjective fear analysis. The RPD ignored the Minister's submission about credibility without providing reasons.

The Respondent's testimony is presumed to be true unless there are good reasons to doubt it. I reviewed the documentary evidence filed and note that it is extensive, and includes supporting medical reports. Identity documents were attached to the supporting statements. Her testimony at the hearing was consistent. Although the psychiatric report can help assess her testimony that she did not disclose the truth about the previous use of a false passport, this allowance can only reasonably be extended to the port of entry. She testified that she was depressed and afraid. The fact that she did not disclose the use of a false passport to a CBSA officer at the airport can be accounted for on this basis. However, the Respondent was represented by counsel when she drafted and filed the Basis of Claim (BOC). Depression and fear cannot reasonably account for her failure to disclose pertinent details to her lawyer for inclusion in the BOC. Her explanation does not adequately respond to the question of why she failed to disclose this information on her own accord, even after taking the psychiatric report into consideration. The RPD erred in failing to draw an adverse credibility inference from this and to include it in its credibility assessment.

After reviewing the documentary evidence, I find no other problems that would put the reliability of testimony and documentary evidence into question. Her oral testimony was internally consistent and supported by a significant amount of reliable evidence, including medical reports. The adverse inference drawn from the use of the forged passport is insufficient to rebut the presumption of truth in this case. Although the RPD erred in its assessment of this issue, my independent assessment leads me to conclude that the Respondent is likely telling the truth about mistreatment in Georgia. The RPD was correct in its conclusion, despite having erred in its evaluation of credibility. The Positions of the Parties with respect to Exclusion The Minister's Intervention

The Notice of Intervention filed by the Minister prior to the hearing alleges that the Respondent committed crimes that, if committed in Canada, would be offences under sections 403 and 57 of the Criminal Code of Canada (CCC). The first concerns personation that is punishable with imprisonment not exceeding ten years. The second concerns the use of a forged passport that can result in imprisonment for up to fourteen years. The Minister cites the Febles decision of the Supreme Court of Canada to submit that these offences are serious for purposes of article 1F(b) exclusion because of the potential length of the jail terms.2

The Minister then cites section 133 of the IRPA that provides that a person may not be charged with an offence under sections 57 or 403 of the CCC, pending the outcome of the refugee claim, if they came to Canada directly or indirectly from the country of alleged persecution.

The Minister relied on the Uppal decision of the Federal Court to submit that section 133 affords protection from prosecution to those who use false passports in order to make their way to Canada to claim asylum.3 The Minister submits that this exception does not apply to the Respondent because her use of the first forged passport did not take place in relation to her arrival in Canada in the course of her current claim for protection, nor does the evidence establish that she used the passport to claim asylum in Canada. The RPD Decision

The RPD did not agree with the Minister's submissions. The panel reasoned that the Respondent would have made it to Canada with the false Canadian passport if she had not been turned back in Cuba. Consequently, she would have benefited from the section 133 exemption if she had not been intercepted en route to Canada and returned to Georgia. The legal principle is the same as was the case when she arrived in Canada with a false Slovakian passport and was not prosecuted because of the operation of section 133. Consequently, the RPD declined to exclude the Respondent on the basis that she did not commit a crime before entering Canada. The Grounds of Appeal by the Minister

The Minister objects to this decision for the following reasons. First, the section 133 exemption is not applicable because the Respondent was not successful in reaching Canada with the first forged passport. The Minister again cites Uppal in support of the submission that the exception only applies to those who use false travel documents in order to enter Canada. The Minister also cites the Federal Court Kathirgamathamby decision, in which the section 133 exception was not extended to a person who used a forged passport to enter the United States because the exception only applies if the fraudulent document was used to enter Canada.4 The Ontario Court of Justice and Ontario Court of Appeal Mossavat decisions are cited in support of the proposition that the correct statutory interpretation of section 133 restricts the exemption to those who enter Canada physically.5

The Minister submits that the RPD erred in law when it found that the exception would have applied if she had arrived in Canada. Section 133 cannot be used retroactively, as the panel believed that it could. Parliament did not intend to extend this protection to offences relating to forged travel documents that occurred at any time and in any place in the past. To do so would undermine the purpose of article 1F(b) exclusion. The Respondent's Reply

The Respondent submits that the Minister's interpretation of section 133 is incompatible with the principles of refugee law and with Canada's international human rights commitments. She used the first passport for no other reason than to seek asylum in Canada. Her failure to arrive in Canada does not alter the purpose with which she used the passport.

The Respondent distinguishes the Uppal decision because that case concerned the use of a fraudulent driver's licence that was not used to gain admission to Canada. Of note is the fact that the court found that the passport was entitled to the benefit of the section 133 exemption.

The Respondent also distinguishes the Kathirgamathamby decision from the facts of the appeal. This case concerned a person who used a false passport to enter the United States. Although he came to Canada to claim asylum after he was released from detention, he never stated that he used the fraudulent travel document with the intention of seeking asylum in Canada.

The Respondent submits that section 133 concerns the purpose of the travel, not whether or not the person was successful in reaching Canada. Because the Respondent used the first fraudulent passport for the sole purpose of seeking asylum in Canada, section 133 applies.

The Respondent cites principles of statutory interpretation in support of the submission that section 133 must be interpreted in light of Canada's international human rights obligations.6 Exclusion of a person who used a fraudulent travel document to seek refugee protection in Canada because the trip was not successful would lead to an absurd result that is inconsistent with international human rights law and with the objectives of the IRPA. The intent of section 133 was to ensure that those who seek asylum in Canada are not prosecuted for using fraudulent documents to do so.

The Respondent goes on to submit that an article 1F(b) analysis must consider the seriousness of the offence.7 The Federal Court Tabagua decision is cited in support to the submission that, even if the section 133 exception did not apply, the first use of a false travel document under these circumstances should not be considered to be serious for purposes of exclusion from refugee protection.8 The RPD did not err in declining to exclude the Respondent

The Interpretation Act (the Act) deems the IRPA to be remedial in nature. In order to achieve this result, consideration of the Act's objectives needs to be done in the context of a "fair, large and liberal construction" of the statute.9 The legislature is presumed not to intend absurd, ridiculous or frivolous consequences, nor an interpretation that is extremely unreasonably, inequitable, illogical, incoherent or incompatible with other provisions of the Act or with the object of the legislative enactment.10 The Supreme Court of Canada cited Elmer Driedger with approval in holding that a statute may not be interpreted on the basis of its wording alone: Today there is only one principle or approach, namely, the words of an Act are to be read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament.11

The Supreme Court of Canada has also referred to this approach as being "contextual and purposive."12 The Court specifically considered the purpose of the IRPA in interpreting its transitional provisions with respect to appeal rights.13

The Federal Court Uppal decision concerns an Immigration Division (ID) Admissibility Hearing about whether the person concerned committed a crime by entering Canada with a false passport and driver's licence to make a refugee claim. The ID concluded that the individual is not inadmissible for having come to Canada with a false passport because of section 133, but that this protection does not extend to the driver's licence. The Court rejected the submission that protection from prosecution afforded by section 133 to passports should be extended to driver's licences on the basis of principles of purposive statutory interpretation. The Court rejected this argument and upheld the ID's determination. The Court stated at paragraphs 21 and 22: 21. On a plain reading of the provision, the protection extends to documents "in relation to the coming into Canada of the person". The intent is to allow bona fide refugees and refugee claimants to use false passports and supporting documents obtained by them for the purpose of making their way into Canada and to shelter them from a finding of inadmissibility for holding and using those documents. 22. In examining the question of inadmissibility, the ID determined that an individual could be sheltered from a finding of inadmissibility only in relation to a fraudulent document that was obtained for the purpose of entering Canada. In my view, that interpretation is correct.

The court considered the objectives of IRPA pertaining to public safety and criminality before concluding that section 133 cannot be extended to prevent prosecution for offences that were committed "for purposes wholly unrelated to fleeing persecution, to enter Canada."14 For this reason, section 133 does not prevent prosecution in the case of the use of a fraudulent driver's licence for a number of years in the United Kingdom unrelated to seeking asylum in Canada.

The Federal Court Kathirgamathamby decision concerned a fraud conviction in the United States for having entered with country with a forged passport.15 After coming to Canada, his application for permanent residency was rejected on the grounds that the previous conviction rendered him inadmissible. The Court allowed the judicial review application on the basis that the equivalency analysis was seriously flawed. By way of obiter dictum, the Court relied on Uppal in stating that section 133 protection would not have applied because the passport in question was used to enter the United States, not Canada. At paragraph 17 the Court notes that this section "could shield a person from a finding of inadmissibility only if the document was used for the purpose of entering Canada." Neither of the cases dealt with the situation of a person prosecuted in another country while in transit to Canada to claim asylum. The Kathirgamathamby case concerns paragraph 36(1)(b) inadmissibility for having been convicted of a foreign offence outside of Canada outside the context of travel to Canada to make a refugee claim. As a result, the two cases are distinguishable from the case on appeal.

The Federal Court considered the Kathirgamathamby decision more recently in the Bellevue case and concluded that the comments pertaining to section 133 constitute non-binding obiter dictum.16 This case concerned an admissibility hearing conducted by the ID based on a conviction in the United States for use of a fraudulent passport that was said to have been used to seek asylum in that country. The ID applied the Court's reasoning in the Kathirgamathamby decision in concluding that section 133 immunity does not apply because the person concerned never entered Canada, even if it were true that a false document was used to enter the U.S. to claim asylum. The Court held that the ID erred in concluding that it was bound by principles of stare decisis because the Court's comments constitute obiter dictum that are not part of the binding ratio decidendi of the decision. As a result, the ID committed a reviewable error in failing to include the applicability of section 133 immunity it its equivalency analysis of Canadian law.

The Uppal decision is not on point because it concerned the use of a fraudulent driver's licence unrelated to seeking asylum in Canada. The Kathirgamathamby case did not concern travel to Canada to claim asylum and is not binding in accordance with principles of stare decisis. Furthermore, the Court opined that section 133 immunity from prosecution could apply in circumstances in which the fraudulent travel document was used "for purposes of entering Canada." In the context of admissibility or prosecution, the purpose for which one obtained and used the travel document before physically arriving in Canada is a relevant consideration for a section 133 assessment. However, the legal issue concerns immunity from prosecution for a past crime, not whether section 133 acts as a defense that entitles one to an acquittal.

Section 133 jurisprudence concerns immunity from prosecution in Canada for the use of fraudulent document to travel to and enter to claim asylum. Article 1F(b) exclusion is a matter of international criminal law as applied in the context of refugee law. Immunities from prosecution are appropriately dealt with as mitigating factors for purposes of determining the seriousness of the offence, not as a defence that leads to the conclusion that no offence was committed.

The refugee protection provisions of the IRPA incorporate an international convention to which Canada is a State party. Article 32 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties provides that recourse may be made to supplementary means of interpreting treaty obligations, including preparatory work of the treaty and the circumstances of its conclusion, in cases where the wording of the treaty is ambiguous or obscure, or if a possible interpretation would lead to a result that is manifestly absurd or unreasonable.17 Article 31 of the Convention requires that treaties be "interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the terms of the treaty in the context and in the light of its object and purpose."

The Supreme Court of Canada accepted the applicability of Article 32 of the Vienna Convention to assist in the interpretation of Article 1F(c) of the Refugee Convention in accordance with section 98 exclusion in the Pushpanathan case.18 The issue of Canada's international obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child for purposes of deciding applications for permanent residency on humanitarian and compassionate grounds was considered by the Supreme Court of Canada in the Baker decision.19 The Court followed previous jurisprudence in holding that international treaties do not form part of Canadian law, unless expressly implemented by statute. Notwithstanding this conclusion, the Court held that the values found in international human rights law can help to inform a contextual approach to statutory interpretation. For this reason, the underlying principles of the Convention on the Rights of the Child may be used for purposes of interpreting the content of humanitarian and compassionate considerations when children are involved.

Supreme Court of Canada jurisprudence requires that ambiguities arising from the incorporation of Canada's obligation under the 1951 Convention regarding the status of refugees be considered in light of the objectives of IPRA and within the broader context of international refugee and human rights law.

Subsection 3(2) of the IRPA outlines the Act's objectives with respect to refugees: a) to recognize that the refugee program is in the first instance about saving lives and offering protection to the displaced and persecuted; (b) to fulfil Canada's international legal obligations with respect to refugees and affirm Canada's commitment to international efforts to provide assistance to those in need of resettlement; (h) to promote international justice and security by denying access to Canadian territory to persons, including refugee claimants, who are security risks or serious criminals.

Article 1F(b) exclusion concerns whether there are serious reasons for considering that the person committed a serious non-political crime prior to admission to the country. This concerns international refugee law as incorporated into the IRPA, not strictly one of Canadian criminal law. International refugee law permits an asylum-seeker to travel with fraudulent documents directly to a country of asylum without risk of facing criminal charges, provided that the person reports to authorities and provides an adequate explanation for the necessity of having done so.

Article 31 of the Refugee Convention provides the following: 1. The Contracting States shall not impose penalties, on account of their illegal entry or presence, on refugees who, coming directly from a territory where their life or freedom was threatened in the sense of article 1, enter or are present in their territory without authorization, provided they present themselves without delay to the authorities and show good cause for their illegal entry or presence.

Guy Goodwin-Gill has provided a detailed assessment of the drafting history and national implementation of this article.20 Discussions among the State parties and in proposals found in the travaux préparatoires show that the State parties were concerned about asylum shopping and the secondary relocation of those who had been determined to be Convention refugees. If an asylum-seeker passes through third countries without legal documentation before arriving in the country of asylum, good reasons must be provided promptly as to why they were either at risk in the transit countries or they could not have obtained temporary protection in any of them. The phrase "coming directly from a territory in which life or freedom was threatened" can include a transit country, and allows for passage through countries in which temporary asylum is not available. This is reflected in the wording of section 133 in IRPA that qualifies that the travel can be either direct or indirect. Goodwin-Gill argues that the term "directly" should not be strictly construed, but should be assessed in light of all of the relevant facts of the case, including the question of risk at various stages of the trip. "Good cause" can include the asylum-seekers understanding of the situation, lack of knowledge of procedures, or actions or instructions from a third party.21 He also submits that to impose penalties for illegal entry without regard to merits of the claim would violate human rights obligations under the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights, as well as regional human rights instruments. Goodwin-Gill notes that the term "penalties" is not defined, but appears to refer to prosecution, fine and imprisonment or administrative detention that is not required.22

The drafting history of Article 31 of the Refugee Convention shows that the State parties were dealing with the question of prosecution under domestic law of asylum seekers who arrived without legal documentation. The discussion and draft version of this article concern the imposition of penalties on those who arrived without legal documentation, not whether their conduct was criminal or otherwise illegal in nature. In other words, the purpose of Article 31 was not to serve as a defence against criminal culpability, but rather to afford immunity from prosecution for a criminal offence. The article does not stipulate that a refugee who enters a country with a forged passport is not guilty of the offence, but rather that the State should refrain from prosecuting the individual, if a good explanation for the conduct can be provided.

Legal defences are relevant to the question of whether a criminal act was committed. Immunity from prosecution does not imply that the conduct was not illegal, but rather that public policy considerations weigh against proceeding with charges. Section 133 of the IRPA is preceded by the rubric "Prosecution of Offences." It specifies that asylum-seekers may not be charged with an offence in relation to the coming into Canada with false documents, pending the outcome of the refugee claim. It is limited in its scope to prosecution in Canada of those who are physically present in the jurisdiction of Canadian prosecutors and courts. It in no way provides a defence that would entitle an acquittal. This perspective is reflected in the Federal Court decisions that have been previously discussed. The issue of inadmissibility before the Immigration Division in paragraph 36(1)(b) case concerns the equivalency of Canadian law with the law of the foreign conviction. The Federal Court case previously considered concerns whether entering the United States with false documents to seek asylum there is equivalent to entering Canada with false documents to claim asylum. In that context, immunity from prosecution is a relevant factor to consider in establishing an equivalency between the two offences, even though it does not concern a legal defence. As a result, this has no direct application to the question of whether a past offence has been committed for purposes of article 1F(b) exclusion.

The legal error that the parties made in the case under appeal lies in confusing immunities with defences. Article 1F(b) exclusion concerns whether the claimant committed serious non- political crimes prior to admission to the country of refuge. Personation and use of a forged passport are serious crimes from the perspective of the Criminal Code of Canada. Section 133 cannot serve as a defence that could lead to the conclusion that no offence was committed. The language of this section concerns the prosecution in Canada of those who are physically present in the country, not to whether document fraud is a serious criminal offence. The RPD erred in concluding that the Jayasekara/ Febles factors did not need to be considered because no offence had been committed. The correct legal approach would have been to conduct an article 1F(b) exclusion assessment on the basis of the factors mandated by the Federal Court of Appeal, as affirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada.23 A discussion of IRPA section 133 could have taken place in the context of mitigating circumstances.

In the alternative, the RPD noted that, even if section 133 did not apply to absolve the Respondent from criminal culpability, the particular facts of the case lead to the conclusion that her conduct cannot be characterized as being serious for purposes of exclusion. No reasons were given and no Jayeasakara analysis was conducted.

The RAD has a mandate to review RPD decision on the basis of correctness, and to correct and re-determine the case, unless evidence would need to be heard by the RPD. In this case, the parties agree to the underlying facts with respect to the use of the forged passport. The issue is the correct interpretation and application of the law. My independent review of the appeal leads me to conclude that the RPD did not err in its conclusion that the Respondent's conduct is not sufficiently serious to warrant exclusion from refugee protection. My reasons follow.

After submitting that no crime was committed by virtue of section 133 of the IRPA, the Respondent submits in the alternative that the RPD failed to assess the claim in accordance with the Jayasekara/Febles factors. The Federal Court Tabagua decision is cited in support of the submission that the RPD failed to consider her conduct as a mitigating factor in this assessment.24 I agree with this submission. Jayasekara/ Febles Factors Elements of the Crime

The Respondent has admitted to have engaged in conduct that meets the basic elements of the crime. With respect to section 403 of the CCC, she fraudulently personated a Canadian citizen with the intent "to avoid arrest or prosecution or to obstruct, prevent or defeat the course of justice." In this case, she intended to use the forged passport in order to defeat the provisions of the IRPA that would have prevented her from travelling to Canada. For purposes of section 57 of the IRPA, she knew that the passport was forged and used it in an attempt to cause others to deal with it as if it were genuine. The elements of the crimes described in sections 57 and 403 of the CCC apply to the Respondent. The Mode of Prosecution

The use of a forged passport under section 57 of the CCC is prosecuted by means of indictment only. Personation pursuant to section 403 of the CCC is a hybrid offence that can be prosecuted either as a summary conviction offence or as an indictable offence. Of the two, the CCC treats the use of a forged passport more seriously than identity fraud, both procedurally and with respect to the maximum sentence. The Penalty Prescribed

Passport fraud under section 57 is punishable with imprisonment not exceeding fourteen years. Personation can result in a term of imprisonment not exceeding ten years if it is prosecuted as an indictable offence. Of the two, the CCC treats the use of a forged passport more seriously than identity fraud, both procedurally and with respect to the maximum sentence. The Facts

The RPD accepted as being true that the Respondent obtained and used the forged Canadian passport for the sole purpose of making a refugee claim in Canada. In light of the preceding credibility assessment, I have no good reason to doubt this. Mitigating and Aggravating Circumstances

Section 133 is one factor among others that can be taken into consideration with respect to the seriousness of the crime for purposes of Article 1F(b) exclusion. Subsection 3(2) of the IRPA at paragraphs (g) and (h) outlines two of the objectives of the Act with respect to refugees. The first goal is to protect the safety and security of Canadian society, and the second is to deny entry to serious criminals or security risks in order to promote international justice and security. Paragraph (b) requires that this be done in the context of respect for Canada's international legal obligations.

As previously discussed, international refugee law allows asylum-seekers to make use of false travel documents in order to seek asylum in a safe third country. Although travel must be direct, allowances are made for passage through unsafe counties or those in which refugee protection is not reasonably available. Canada extended this principle in section 133 of the IRPA to allow for indirect travel. Although this provision is not directly applicable to Article 1F(b) exclusion, the international human rights context indicates that travel with false travel documents for the purpose of seeking asylum is not a serious offence.

The UNHCR Refugee Status Determination Handbook notes that it is difficult to define what a serious non-political crime is for purposes of exclusion. Minor crimes punishable by moderate sentences do not suffice. They must either be a capital crime or a "very grave punishable act."25 Aggravating circumstances such as previous criminal convictions may be taken into account. The UNHCR Handbook notes at paragraph 158 that some crimes may be committed in order for a refugee to leave the country of persecution. For example, it may be possible to overlook crashing a stolen car through border control, but it becomes more difficult to accept if an asylum-seeker hijacks an aircraft.

The Respondent has no criminal record and made use of one forged travel document in an attempt to seek asylum in Canada. She does not pose a danger to the public, nor to the security of Canada. She committed the offence in order to flee persecution. However, her lack of truthfulness about the false passport is an aggravating factor. The Respondent did not disclose the use of the forged passport until confronted by the CBSA, despite the assistance of a lawyer. The principle behind the immunity from prosecution under the Refugee Convention requires that one disclose the illegal conduct promptly to authorities and to provide a reasonable explanation at that time. Although not directly applicable, the fact that she failed to respect the obligation to report is an aggravating factor in the context of international law.
The parties did not cite Canadian case law with respect to the way Canadian criminal courts have sentenced similarly-situated persons.

When the mitigating and aggravating factors are considered in light international refugee and human rights law principles and in the context of the Jayasekara/ Febles factors, I conclude that the offence committed is not sufficiently serious to warrant exclusion under Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention. If a forged passport were used for purposes other than to seek asylum in Canada, the particular facts of the case would need to be considered in order to determine the seriousness of the offence. In the case under appeal, the purpose for which it was used is determinative of the conclusion that it was not sufficiently serious to warrant exclusion from refugee protection. Although the Minister is correct that section 133 immunity is not directly applicable to the Respondent's situation, especially given that fact that she did not disclose the truth in a timely manner as required by Article 31 of the Refugee Convention, the underlying principle supports the conclusion that this offence is not of sufficiently serious nature to warrant exclusion.
Despite my conclusion that the RPD erred in its failure to conduct an assessment using the legally-mandated factors, I agree with its final determination.

I agree with the Minister that the RPD erred by failing to take the Respondent's lack of honesty about the forged passport into consideration in the credibility assessment. In addition, the RPD erred in misinterpreting the applicability of section 133 of the IRPA and by failing to conduct a Jayasekara/ Febles assessment as it was required to do. However, my independent evaluation of the appeal leads me to conclude that the RPD's finding that the Respondent is telling the truth about past persecution in Georgia is likely true and that past criminal conduct does not meet the criteria set out in the prescribed factors to warrant exclusion. Although I agree with the Minister that the RPD erred in its treatment of section 133 and in its failure to consider the Respondent's lack of truthfulness in its credibility assessment, I concur with the outcome.

Despite the mistakes made by the RPD, the conclusion that the Respondent is a Convention refugee who is not excluded from protection by operation of Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention is correct.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is a Convention refugee who is not excluded from refugee protection by operation of Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
